sections.title: DISCUSSION
sections.text:
Issued at 159 AM EDT Tue Sep 22 2026

Over the next 48 hours a rex block pattern will take shape over the 
eastern CONUS, with an upper low deepening over the Ohio valley and 
central Appalachian region and the upper high to its north 
strengthening over the Canadian side of the Great Lakes region. 
Meanwhile, surface high pressure develops beneath the ridge over the 
Great Lakes which will help to push a weak front, which was situated 
from West Virginia southwest into the Cumberland Plateau this 
evening, southward through the area sometime late Tuesday afternoon 
and evening. All of this will result in continued scattered to 
numerous shower and thunderstorm activity across the region through 
late Wednesday evening, with the best coverage during diurnally 
favored daytime hours but also with lingering convection during the 
overnight hours. For Tuesday, with the boundary slowly shifting 
south, the threat of any strong to severe storms should largely be 
relegated to the far southern TN valley and our western NC counties. 
However, PWATs will remain elevated through Wednesday, and storm 
motions very slow, so an isolated flooding threat could exist 
virtually anywhere through that period, though in general the 
risk of flooding should shift south with time as well.

Speaking of Wednesday, the pattern change really gets underway late 
Wednesday. The upper low associated with the rex block pattern, 
dives east southeast to the coastal Carolina region Wednesday night 
into Thursday, allowing for persistent northerly flow to spread 
across the CWA, ushering in significantly cooler and drier air. 
We'll still be warm on Wednesday, with highs in the mid to upper 80s 
south of I-40. But Thursday through the weekend will see highs 
topping out largely in the 70s, except the far southern TN valley 
which may still manage to best the 80 degree mark each day. Perhaps 
the more important note will be overnight lows in the 40s and 50s 
Friday night onward.

enso.title: ENSO Alert System Status: El Niño Advisory
paragraphs: ENSO Alert System Status: El Niño Advisory Synopsis: El Niño is strengthening, with a greater than 90% chance of a very strong event during the Northern Hemisphere fall and winter 2026-27. El Niño strengthened further over the past month, with sea surface temperature anomalies exceeding +3.0°C in the eastern equatorial Pacific [Fig. 1] . Except for the Niño-4 index, which decreased to +0.1°C in August, values in the other Niño indices increased, reaching +1.8°C in Niño-3.4, +2.5°C in Niño-3, and +3.4°C in Niño-1+2 [Fig. 2] . The equatorial subsurface temperature index (average from 180°-100°W) remained steady during August [Fig. 3] , reflecting a deeper-than-average thermocline [Fig. 4] . Subsurface temperatures continued to be significantly above average, with widespread anomalies in excess of +10.0°C at depth. Low-level westerly wind anomalies and upper-level easterly wind anomalies extended from the western to the east-central equatorial Pacific. Enhanced convection and rainfall persisted from the central to the eastern Pacific, while anomalies remained suppressed over Indonesia [Fig. 5] . The traditional and equatorial Southern Oscillation indices remained negative. Collectively, the coupled ocean-atmosphere system reflected a strengthening El Niño. The CPC Official ENSO outlook , which synthesizes multiple models from North America and abroad, indicates El Niño will continue to strengthen through the end of the year [Figs. 6

-8] . During the October-December 2026 season, there is a 75% chance of a historic event that would exceed the strength of previous El Niño events dating back to 1950 (+2.5°C or more for a 3-month RONI value ). With an event of this magnitude, the chances of experiencing impacts consistent with El Niño are larger, though not guaranteed (see CPC outlooks for probabilities of seasonal anomalies). In summary, El Niño is strengthening, with a greater than 90% chance of a very strong event during the Northern Hemisphere fall and winter 2026-27. This discussion is a consolidated effort of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), NOAA's National Weather Service, and their funded institutions. md.summary: Strong wind gusts may affect parts of the Metroplex later this evening. Isolated damaging gusts cannot be ruled out.
md.discussion: A cluster of storms that formed in southern OK continues to push south/southeast across the Red River, with the stronger storm moving through Gainesville TX. Other cells are also developing along the outflow, extending into northern Wise and Jack counties. Meanwhile, an older outflow boundary is pushing north and extends from Dallas to Hood counties. This area has become relatively hot today, with upper 90s to near 100 F temperatures. Surface analysis also indicates a low between the storms to the north and northward-moving outflow to the south. Given the steep low level lapse rates ahead of these storms (which are substantial in height), and possibility of increased surface convergence/colliding outflows, it seems possible at least strong outflow will affect the Metroplex later this evening, with perhaps locally damaging gusts assuming storm cores continue to develop as they approach out of the north.
